pitch: The software company has already found the customers, your job is making sure the tool actually works for them, which many businesses struggle to do alone.
best: Someone willing to commit to deeply learning one specific software platform before expecting to earn from it.
truth: A reasonable, learnable model, but it does require a real time investment becoming genuinely expert in one platform before the first client, this isn't a same-week income source.

name: Running several small YouTube channels for combined ad income
what: Rather than building one large channel, run several small, niche YouTube channels at once, blogging, household tips, YouTuber-focused content, and casual chat videos among them, each earning modest AdSense income that together adds up to a livable income.
pitch: The creator shows her real February AdSense breakdown across all eight channels, totaling over €2,000 for the month. Her four biggest channels each bring in a few hundred euros, while four smaller ones bring in under €100 each. She's candid that no single channel would support her: "if I only had one, I wouldn't even reach €1,000."
best: Someone drawn to content creation who values honesty over hype, and who's comfortable with a modest, steady income built from several small sources rather than betting on one channel going viral.
truth: This is one of the more credible, non-hyped accounts in this database precisely because the numbers shown are unglamorous, specific, and shown on-screen in the actual AdSense dashboard rather than just stated. Worth noting the figures are in euros, not dollars, and that running eight channels simultaneously, even small ones, is still real, ongoing content production, not a passive setup.

name: Coaching existing YouTubers on monetization and growth
cost: Low startup cost, needs your own credibility
what: Coach existing YouTubers who already have an audience and expertise, in this case a creator teaching the Amazon KDP publishing model, on monetization, operations, and hiring, packaged as a paid course plus coaching program.
pitch: In a named, on-camera case study, Hummus describes taking his client Sean's channel from around 100,000 subscribers to over 300,000, more than tripling AdSense income to $22,000 a month, growing course revenue to over $500,000 a month, and landing a single affiliate commission of $73,000 along the way.
best: Someone who already has real, demonstrable expertise in a specific area of business or content growth to coach others in, since this model depends entirely on already having that credibility.
truth: This is Hummus's own paying client, interviewed together on camera, which is a stronger transparency signal than a third-party retelling, but it's still a single promotional case study from the coach's own business, not an independently audited result. Building a coaching business requires you to already have real expertise in a specific niche, which isn't something this idea creates for you.

name: A copywriting technique for selling without cold calls
cost: No cost, a skill to learn
what: A messaging framework for selling high-ticket services through content rather than cold outreach: shift from convincing cold leads on sales calls to creating content that pre-sells them, so by the time someone reaches out, they've already decided to work with you.
pitch: Youngs says he grew his own consulting business from zero to over $1 million a year over three years without a sales team and without a single sales call, using this content-first approach instead of traditional outbound selling.
best: Anyone selling a service through content marketing who wants to reduce reliance on cold outreach or sales calls, this is a technique to apply, not a business on its own.
truth: This is Youngs describing his own business's growth, a specific and named claim, but self-reported with no external verification or account data shown. The core idea, that content can do the convincing work sales calls used to do, is a real and increasingly common approach among online service providers, worth learning regardless of which specific business you're building.

name: The 7-11-4 framework for building audience trust
cost: No cost, a technique to apply
found: Daniel Priestley on The Diary Of A CEO
what: A framework describing how audience trust builds: people generally need around 7 hours, 11 interactions, across 4 different platforms total with your content before they feel they genuinely know and trust you, similar to how a parasocial relationship with a celebrity forms, achieved through consistent publishing across multiple channels.
pitch: Priestley grounds this in real psychology research, Dunbar's numbers, the idea that humans can only hold a limited number of people in memory, and argues that hitting roughly 7 hours and 11 interactions across 4 platforms is what moves someone from a stranger to someone who'd recognize and approach you at a conference.
best: Anyone building a personal brand or following as part of a larger business, a supporting technique for audience-building, not a business idea on its own.
truth: The framework is tied to real, named research (Dunbar's numbers) rather than an invented statistic, which is a good credibility signal, though the exact figures (7 hours, 11 interactions, 4 platforms) should be read as a memorable rule of thumb rather than a precisely measured formula. This reframes slow audience growth as expected and cumulative rather than a sign something isn't working.

name: Direct response marketing fundamentals
what: A skills roadmap for mastering persuasive marketing: study old direct-response print ads from the early 1900s for their headline and hook structure, build a personal "swipe file" of proven techniques, then apply that structure to modern ad traffic, distinguishing between demand capture (people already searching for a solution) and demand generation (people who don't yet know they have the problem).
pitch: Suby cites advertising legend David Ogilvy's claim that 80% of his agency's client profits came from direct-response work despite it receiving a minority of the ad budget, and lays out concrete mechanics, a roughly 4% click-through rate is typical on Google search ads, as a starting benchmark for evaluating your own campaigns.
best: Anyone doing marketing, copywriting, or content work who wants a stronger foundation in persuasion and traffic strategy, a skill to build, not a business on its own.
truth: The historical references (Ogilvy, the direct-response advertising era) are real and independently checkable, which lends real credibility to the framework. This is presented as general marketing education rather than tied to selling a specific product in this video, a reasonably trustworthy, low-risk skill to develop regardless of which specific business idea you pursue.

name: A 7-day method for testing app ideas cheaply
cost: $100 to $500 in ad spend to test
what: A methodology, not a specific app, for taking an app idea to a paying customer within one week: research an underserved niche using existing App Store data, build an MVP using Claude Cowork and Claude Code to go from a product requirements doc to working software, then run a small paid-ad budget to test real demand before investing further.
pitch: Malinowski picks an astrology app niche that's dominated by products targeting women, builds a version aimed at men in a few hours using Claude, then spends $100 a day testing it with paid ads. By day six, after fixing a bug that had wiped out an entire day's ad spend with zero signups, he gets 7 new trials for $100 spent, landing under his $20 target cost-per-acquisition for profitability.
best: Someone comfortable with hands-on technical troubleshooting, debugging, and ad account management, not just describing what they want built and waiting.
truth: This is one of the more transparent accounts in this database: Malinowski shows a real failed day, a bug that silently blocked every paywall for 24 hours and wasted $100 in ad spend, rather than only a polished highlight reel. Getting a handful of trial signups in a week is a genuine, useful validation signal, but it's still early-stage evidence, not proof of a sustainable business, and this does require real comfort with iterative technical problem-solving beyond basic AI prompting.

name: A value-first approach to monetizing a newsletter
what: A framework for monetizing an email newsletter: treat it primarily as a way to nurture and add real value to an audience rather than a constant sales channel, focus curation on the top few most relevant items rather than trying to cover everything, and only introduce paid offers once readers are already getting consistent value for free.
pitch: Swigunski says he's built email lists with hundreds of thousands of subscribers that have generated hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue, and frames the newsletter's core job as warming up an audience so that when a paid offer does appear, people already trust the sender enough to buy.
best: Anyone already running, or considering, an email newsletter as part of a business, a methodology to apply, not a standalone idea by itself.
truth: The "hundreds of millions in revenue" figure is a broad, self-reported career claim without account-level detail to verify it, so treat it as a credibility signal rather than an audited number. The underlying approach, curate tightly, lead with value, sell only once trust is established, is a solid, well-established newsletter strategy independent of that headline figure, and results still depend heavily on actually growing a real, engaged subscriber base.

name: White-label SaaS reseller for local business niches (GoHighLevel)
cost: Low startup cost (~$497/month software fee, plus ad spend)
found: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
what: You white-label GoHighLevel's all-in-one marketing and CRM software and resell it to local business niches (event rental companies, med spas, gyms, dentists, roofers, and similar), charging a monthly software fee while your own reseller cost stays fixed at $497 a month regardless of how many clients you have.
pitch: Koerner reverse-engineers real competitors using GoHighLevel's own public "SaaSpreneur" awards page, which shows which resellers have crossed 100, 500, or 1,000+ paying customers, then walks through a five-tool toolkit: the pricing page, the Wayback Machine, the Meta Ads Library, builtwith.com, and LinkedIn, to estimate a competitor's real revenue, ad spend, and team size. He demonstrates the model live by building a "missed call text back" tool for a roofing business in a few minutes inside GoHighLevel, showing how a small wedge product can turn into a broader retainer relationship.
best: Someone comfortable with sales and marketing research who's willing to pick one underserved local-business niche and specialize in it, rather than trying to serve every industry at once.
truth: Koerner discloses upfront that he's a GoHighLevel affiliate and earns a commission if viewers sign up through his link, worth keeping in mind given how enthusiastically the software is framed. All of the specific revenue estimates for the example businesses are his own "back of a napkin" math based on public award tiers and pricing pages, not verified financials, a reasonable estimate but not an audited number. The reverse-engineering toolkit itself is genuinely useful and independently verifiable regardless of how accurate any single revenue guess turns out to be.

name: Portable sanitation servicing (porta-potties and construction site rentals)
cost: Significant upfront equipment cost (units plus servicing truck)
what: Rent and service portable toilets and sanitation units for active construction sites, which are legally required to have them for the length of a build, as well as weddings, festivals, and outdoor events, charging a recurring monthly or per-visit fee to pump out, restock, and maintain each unit.
pitch: Construction contracts alone can run 6 to 18 months and combine a monthly per-unit rental fee with weekly service visits, and the same units can also be booked for single-weekend events, giving two very different customer bases for the same physical asset. The presenters argue this is one of the most recession-proof businesses on their list, since active construction and events don't stop needing sanitation just because almost nobody wants to be the one servicing it.
best: Someone willing to do genuinely unglamorous, hands-on labor (or manage a crew that does), and who has the capital to purchase the units as a real upfront equipment cost.
truth: The presenters are candid that this is deliberately ranked near the bottom of their list specifically because it's the least glamorous, most labor-intensive business on it, since you or your crew are doing the pump-outs and restocks yourselves. They frame it as a legitimate, demand-backed business rather than a passive one, and don't overstate how easy it is to get started.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Small engine repair shop
what: Repair small engines, lawnmowers, generators, chainsaws, pressure washers, and line striping machines, for local landscaping crews, contractors, and homeowners, positioning yourself as the reliable shop with fast turnaround rather than a hobbyist who fixes engines occasionally.
pitch: The presenters argue this is a skilled trade that almost nobody under 50 is actively pursuing, even though every contractor with small engine equipment eventually needs it fixed and there's no national chain to call. The real opportunity, they say, isn't that nobody fixes engines, it's that almost nobody does it as a real, reliable business with an actual shop and same-day callbacks.
best: Someone younger who's willing to learn a genuine skilled trade and is comfortable with a business that gets noticeably slower in winter, since demand is seasonal for outdoor equipment.
truth: The presenters are upfront that this is one of the weaker "build a real business" plays on their list precisely because the labor takes real time to learn and the seasonality is a real constraint. It's framed as a good cash-flow trade, not an easy path to a scalable company.

name: Fire extinguisher testing and inspection route
what: Inspect and tag fire extinguishers for offices, restaurants, warehouses, and apartment buildings on the legally required annual inspection schedule, building up a recurring route of accounts over time.
pitch: Every commercial building is legally required to get its extinguishers inspected on a set schedule, and fire marshals actually check for the tag, which means the law itself does the sales pitch for you. Once you're inspecting a building's extinguishers, switching to a new inspector means a customer has to re-explain their whole building to someone new, which the presenters say makes accounts unusually sticky once you land them.
best: Someone comfortable with slower, longer commercial sales cycles who's willing to build up a large route of low-ticket accounts over time rather than looking for one big score.
truth: The presenters are honest that this sits mid-list specifically because it isn't high-ticket per visit, so building meaningful income requires a genuinely large route and patience with commercial sales cycles. They note it's a fragmented market with no dominant national brand, a real and checkable structural fact about the industry.

name: Commercial dock and door equipment service
cost: Moderate to high startup cost (specialized tools, van)
what: Repair and maintain the dock levelers, roll-up doors, and dock seals that every warehouse and distribution center relies on to load and unload trucks, and sign accounts to quarterly preventive-maintenance contracts.
pitch: When a loading bay breaks, a warehouse can't load or unload trucks, so operators will pay premium rates for same-day emergency repair on top of standard preventive-maintenance contracts. The presenters point to the ongoing warehouse and e-commerce boom as a structural tailwind that keeps this market growing every year.
best: Someone with real electrical and hydraulic know-how, since this is effectively a skilled trade working with motors, sensors, and safety systems, not a business you can outsource entirely from day one.
truth: The presenters rank this in the middle of their list specifically because of the technical skill and safety risk involved, since it's your hands doing the diagnosing and fixing unless you eventually buy your way into an existing operation. They're clear this isn't a laptop business.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Waste oil and grease collection and recycling route
what: Collect used motor oil and cooking grease from auto shops, restaurants, and small manufacturers on a recurring pickup schedule, a regulatory requirement for these businesses, then resell the collected oil to re-refiners for a second revenue stream on the same stop.
pitch: Businesses that generate used oil or grease can't legally dispose of it themselves, so pickup isn't optional, and once you're the hauler of record for an account, the presenters say customers rarely shop around since nobody wants to risk getting caught non-compliant. The double revenue stream, a pickup fee plus reselling the oil, is what the presenters say sets this apart from most other route-based businesses on their list.
best: Someone with access to real startup capital for a vacuum truck and the right hauling permits, and who's comfortable with revenue that partly fluctuates with commodity oil prices.
truth: The presenters flag this honestly as one of the heaviest startup-cost items on their list, requiring a specialized vehicle and permits before you can legally operate, and note the resale side of the revenue moves with oil prices rather than staying flat. They frame it as one of the least-known businesses on the list rather than a proven, widely replicated model.
situation_tags: Needs a truck or cargo vehicle

name: Truck driver recruiting and placement service
cost: Very low startup cost (ad spend only)
what: Run Facebook ads to find qualified CDL drivers and owner-operators looking for better freight or routes, vet them for a valid license and clean record, then place them with trucking companies for a per-driver placement fee.
pitch: Trucking companies lose real money, cited at around $4,000 a month per truck, for every truck sitting empty without a qualified driver, which is why carriers will pay a placement fee of up to $4,000 for every qualified driver who gets hired and stays on. The presenters describe this as one of the purest "laptop style" businesses on their list, since you never touch a truck, own a truck, or need labor, inventory, or a lease, just a Facebook ad account.
best: Someone comfortable running paid ads and doing consistent outreach, since this is a placement/staffing model rather than a subscription, meaning you're always selling and refilling the pipeline, and a slow month directly hits revenue.
truth: The presenters are candid that this ranks mid-list because of that staffing-model instability, not because the underlying opportunity is weak, calling it stressful when the pipeline gets thin. The $4,000-per-truck and per-placement figures come from a source the presenter says they spoke with directly, a specific and checkable-in-principle number, though it's a single secondhand account rather than an audited industry statistic.

name: Non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT) service
what: Coordinate rides for patients who need regular transportation to dialysis, chemotherapy, or other medical appointments and can't drive themselves, billing the ride to Medicaid or insurance rather than charging the patient directly, while independent drivers with their own vehicles do the actual driving.
pitch: Because rides bill through insurance rather than a rideshare-style flat rate, the presenters say pricing runs meaningfully higher than a service like Uber, and recurring patients, such as someone needing dialysis three times a week for years, create some of the stickiest repeat revenue on their whole list. Once a patient and their case manager trust a driver, the presenters argue they're unlikely to go looking for a new one.
best: Someone with patience for paperwork and a willingness to navigate Medicaid and managed-care billing, plus the operational discipline to vet and manage independent drivers as the actual face of the service.
truth: The presenters are direct that getting set up to bill Medicaid and insurance is genuinely slow and paperwork-heavy, and that payment itself can take a while to come through, real friction points they don't gloss over. They also flag that driver reliability is the whole product here, since patients are trusting the driver, not the company brand.

name: Foundation repair and waterproofing lead generation
what: Partner with licensed foundation repair and waterproofing crews who already own the specialized equipment, hydraulic piers, drainage systems, and handle their marketing, scheduling, and sales conversations in exchange for a cut of every job you bring them, without doing any of the physical repair work yourself.
pitch: A cracking foundation or a flooding crawl space pushes homeowners to act fast, with jobs commonly running $5,000 to $15,000, and the presenters note there's no single dominant player controlling more than a small share of the market. Because you're leveraging crews who already own expensive equipment, the presenters say you can start with just a Google Business Profile and some before-and-after photos rather than any real capital.
best: Someone comfortable with lead generation and sales who wants to avoid buying equipment or doing physical labor, and who's okay with a business that's mostly one-time transactions per customer rather than recurring.
truth: The presenters are upfront that the one thing keeping this from ranking higher on their list is that it's almost entirely one-time work, a homeowner's foundation gets fixed once, and then you're hoping for the next referral or lead, which they acknowledge can get stressful as you try to grow. They frame the urgency and dollar amounts as genuine, not exaggerated, since a worsening foundation is a real, escalating cost to the homeowner.

name: Remote-run residential cleaning business
what: Run a residential house-cleaning business without doing any of the cleaning yourself. Hire independent cleaners who already own their own supplies and vehicles, handle the marketing, scheduling, and customer relationships, and split revenue roughly 50/50 with the cleaner on every job.
pitch: The presenters rank this their overall number-one pick because it's a large, fragmented home-services market with no dominant national brand, and roughly one in three one-time cleanings converts into a recurring client, building compounding revenue instead of starting from zero every month. Using a rough example, a $350 first-time deep clean split 50/50 with the cleaner, scaled to around 25 to 30 recurring clients, gets to roughly $10,000 a month in revenue with no employees on payroll and minimal ongoing labor from the owner.
best: Someone willing to build the business around recruiting and managing independent cleaners from day one, rather than doing cleanings themselves to save money early on, which the presenters call the single most common way people sabotage this model.
truth: The presenters are explicit that this is the business they'd start themselves from zero, and flag a real failure pattern: people who fail at this almost always fail the same way, by getting personally attached to doing the cleaning and building limiting beliefs around recruiting cleaners instead of stepping into an owner role early. They also promote a paid mentorship program at the end with a stated revenue and client guarantee, worth knowing given the number of specific client success figures cited throughout the video.

name: Free AI-built websites as a client acquisition wedge
cost: Very low startup cost (AI subscription only)
found: The Calum Johnson Show (guest: Jack Roberts)
what: Build a genuinely good website for a local business using AI tools like Claude, give it away completely for free with no strings attached, and use the relationship that builds to become that business's go-to "AI guy", then upsell paid recurring services like SEO, chatbots, or lead-capture dashboards.
pitch: Roberts argues websites are the easiest way to get a first paying client with AI right now, because AI tools can now produce genuinely polished, conversion-focused sites (he cites having personally sold websites for over $10,000) in well under an hour. He walks through the specific process: research what the best-converting websites in a niche have in common using AI, build a free website using that structure for a business with a weak or outdated site, then open the conversation with what else they need, more leads, a better sign-up rate, which naturally leads into paid, recurring work.
best: Someone who's willing to give away real value upfront before asking for anything, and who's comfortable using their existing personal network for a first client. The video cites an internal survey of over 3,000 people in the presenter's community where 80% said their first client came from personal connections, not cold outreach.
truth: The specific tactic here is giving the entire first deliverable away for free as a relationship-building wedge rather than charging for it from the start. The $10,000-website and 80%-personal-network figures are the presenter's own self-reported numbers from his own community, not independently audited, and the interview functions partly as a promotion for the Hermes agent tool and the presenter's paid community, worth factoring in given how enthusiastically both are described.

name: Part-time YouTube channel in your existing expertise, scripted with Claude
cost: Very low startup cost (phone or webcam, AI subscription)
what: Start a YouTube channel in a niche built around your existing job, expertise, or life experience, nursing, HVAC, cybersecurity, whatever you already know, while keeping your day job, using Claude to compress scriptwriting into small pockets of spare time like lunch breaks and commutes instead of the hours it used to take.
pitch: Hummus frames the whole plan as roughly four hours a week: about an hour once a month brainstorming video ideas with Claude, short lunch-break sessions talking through and polishing scripts, a single batch-recording session, and a short publishing session, arguing that AI collapsed what used to require a researcher, writer, strategist, and marketer into one $20-a-month tool. He backs this with several named case studies from his own community; his brother, a 50-year-old HVAC business owner, reportedly went from zero to over $18,000 in a month within his first month of posting.
best: Someone with real existing knowledge or experience in a specific field who's willing to treat this as a slow-burn asset rather than a fast payout, and who has small pockets of otherwise-idle time to work with.
truth: The named examples throughout the video are specific and checkable in principle, a decent transparency signal, but they're all self-reported figures from the presenter's own paid community, not independently verified. The video functions as a funnel into a free live training and, ultimately, a paid one-on-one mentorship program described as "very expensive," worth knowing given how much of the video is built around these specific dollar-figure success stories.

name: Pay-per-lead agency (broker or self-run)
cost: Needs ongoing ad budget (or none, if brokering)
what: Instead of selling marketing services on a retainer, generate qualified leads through Meta ads and a qualifying quiz funnel in a single niche, like life insurance, business loans, or debt settlement, and sell each lead exclusively to a buyer who wants that kind of prospect, or broker leads between existing suppliers and buyers without touching ad spend yourself.
pitch: Robinson argues this beats a traditional retainer agency on two fronts: leads are an easier sell than ongoing "marketing services" because virtually every business owner says yes to more leads, and there are two direct levers to grow profit, raising the price per lead or lowering the cost to generate it. He walks through ten specific verticals with rough sale prices and costs to generate (life insurance around $50 to $60 a lead, mortgage leads $100 to $120, legal leads up to $200 to $250), and recommends beginners start with the lower-risk broker model, sourcing leads from existing suppliers and reselling at a fixed markup, before eventually running their own ad campaigns.
best: Someone with real comfort running or learning to run Meta ad campaigns, or, for the broker path, someone comfortable with B2B cold outreach and negotiating supplier relationships, since neither path is a passive income stream.
truth: Robinson discloses upfront that he's teaching this as a free lead-in to his paid community, and the free version leaves out the detailed funnel templates, scripts, and full campaign structure that are gated behind the paid offer. The specific revenue figures (a $250K+/month agency, 30% average margins) come from his own screenshotted tracking sheet, a more concrete transparency signal than most claims in this space, but still self-reported and not independently audited.

name: AI-generated digital products (Etsy-style templates, trackers, planners)
cost: Low startup cost (AI subscription plus ad testing budget)
what: Use an AI agent (the video uses GenSpark) to research which digital products, planners, trackers, templates, and similar downloadable goods, are already proven sellers on marketplaces like Etsy, generate a polished version yourself, and validate demand with paid ads before fully building the product out.
pitch: The presenter distills the pattern from studying paid sales data on top Etsy digital-product sellers into five habits: validate demand with ads before building, target one specific person and moment rather than a broad audience, send traffic straight to a single-product page with the buy button at the top, show real proof like screenshots and numbers instead of vague promises, and use AI for a first draft that a human then edits rather than selling AI output unedited. He walks through the actual process inside GenSpark, from researching best-selling listings to generating product mockup images for the store listing.
best: Someone comfortable with iterative testing, running small ad spends to validate an idea before investing real time building it out, rather than someone hoping to build the "perfect" product first.
truth: The presenter discloses he's promoting his own affiliate link for GenSpark, and the specific case-study sales figures ($22,000, $16,000, $15,000 in 30 days for individual sellers) come from a paid third-party data tool he says he purchased access to, not something a viewer can verify directly. The underlying five-pattern framework, validate before building, niche down hard, one-page funnels, real proof, AI draft plus human edit, is sound and independently checkable advice regardless of the specific dollar figures shown.

name: AI workflow consultant for local businesses
cost: Very low startup cost (free AI tools)
what: Walk into a local business, a plumber, dental practice, or small agency, and ask three simple questions to find one repetitive task worth automating, then rebuild that task using free or low-cost tools like Claude and Zapier so it runs on its own, charging an upfront audit fee plus an ongoing monthly retainer to keep it running.
pitch: Hawksworth frames the pitch as a simple three-question framework anyone can use on a cold walk-in or call: what task do you do most and hate most, does it follow the same steps every time, and what does an hour of your time actually cost. He suggests charging roughly £1,000 for the initial audit and £300 to £500 a month to maintain the automation, arguing that businesses aren't really buying AI, they're buying relief from stress.
best: Someone comfortable approaching local business owners directly, in person or by phone, and translating a vague complaint about busywork into a specific, sellable automation.
truth: The pricing figures given (£1,000 audit, £300-500/month retainer) are the presenter's own suggested starting points, not verified case studies of what businesses have actually paid him. The three-question diagnostic framework itself is straightforward and genuinely reusable regardless of the specific price points.

name: Private AI assistant built for a solo expert (consultant, solicitor, advisor)
what: Build a private AI assistant for a solo professional, a consultant, solicitor, or financial advisor, by loading their past proposals, FAQs, and other documents into a Claude Project, then instructing it to answer questions and draft new proposals only in that person's own voice and only from their own material.
pitch: Hawksworth demonstrates the entire build in a couple of minutes: start a Claude project, drag in roughly 20 past proposals and FAQs, and give it a single instruction to answer only from the documents provided and ask a clarifying question if the answer isn't there. He suggests charging around £1,500 to build it and £300 a month to maintain it as their workflow grows, framing the value as multiplying the expert's own existing knowledge rather than replacing them.
best: Someone comfortable working with solo professionals who already have a body of past work, proposals, FAQs, case files, to draw from, since the tool is only as good as the material it's trained on.
truth: The pricing (£1,500 build, £300/month) is the presenter's own suggested figure, not a documented sale. The underlying build process itself, a Claude Project scoped to a specific person's documents with a narrow instruction, is simple enough to verify and replicate directly.

name: AI-personalized, trigger-based sales prospecting service
what: Feed Claude a prospect and a specific trigger event, a funding round, a new hire, a relevant post, and have it draft a short, non-pitchy outreach message that references the trigger directly, so a sales team spends less time hunting for leads and writing near-identical cold messages and more time on actual conversations.
pitch: Hawksworth's pitch is that this doesn't replace a sales team, it removes the boring research and first-draft-writing work that eats their week, while keeping the human conversation, which he argues is what actually closes deals, intact. He suggests charging around £1,500 to set the system up and £750 a month to keep it running and the CRM organized.
best: Someone selling into businesses that already have a sales team or process in place and just need the research and outreach-drafting work taken off their plate, rather than businesses with no sales process at all.
truth: The pricing figures (£1,500 setup, £750/month) are the presenter's own suggested starting points, not documented client outcomes. This kind of trigger-based, one-prospect-at-a-time personalization is a specific tactic within the broader AI-powered sales space that shows up across a lot of WAH creator content, and the underlying mechanic, feeding Claude a single prospect and trigger, is simple enough to test yourself before paying for training on it.

name: AI content repurposing service for local businesses
cost: Zero to very low startup cost
what: Take one piece of long-form content a business already has, a podcast episode, webinar, or long video, and use AI to break it into a week or more of social media posts, so a business that made one good piece of content and then let it die gets ongoing distribution from it instead.
pitch: Hawksworth flags this as the idea he'd start with if he had zero clients and zero budget, since it needs no upfront tools or cash, just one business that's already creating content and wasting it. He cites one local business he did this for going from posting once every two weeks to multiple times a day, tripling their inbound inquiries in the process, and suggests using that first free or cheap result as the proof needed to land the next paying client.
best: Someone with genuinely no starting budget who wants a true zero-cost way to get a first result and testimonial, since the pitch here is explicitly to start by doing this for one business for little or nothing.
truth: The "tripled inbound inquiries" figure is a single case study from the presenter's own client work, not an independently verified result, though it's specific enough (once every two weeks to multiple times daily) to be a meaningfully checkable claim if you were working with that same business. The zero-budget, first-client-as-proof structure is a genuinely low-risk way to test the idea before committing any money.

name: AI-powered internal knowledge base for small businesses
what: Load a business's scattered documentation, processes, policies, scripts, and meeting notes, into a Claude Project so the whole team can get instant answers instead of repeatedly interrupting each other or a manager to ask where something is or how something works.
pitch: Hawksworth's argument is that most small businesses already have the knowledge they need, it's just scattered across documents, chats, and people's heads, so the sale isn't "AI," it's making onboarding faster and support more consistent. He suggests charging around £2,000 to build the initial system and £400 a month to keep it updated as the business's documentation changes.
best: Someone comfortable working with a business's existing internal documents and organizing them, more an information-organization skill than a technical one.
truth: The pricing (£2,000 build, £400/month) is the presenter's own suggested figure rather than a documented sale price. The underlying build, loading existing documents into a Claude Project scoped to that business, is simple enough to test on a small scale before committing to a specific price.

name: AI-built landing pages for local businesses (Framer and Claude)
what: Build a modern landing page for a local business, a restaurant, gym, dentist, or estate agent with an old or confusing site, by describing the business to an AI website builder (the video uses Framer, alongside Claude and Claude Code), then doing the human work of sharpening the message and call to action.
pitch: Hawksworth is explicit that AI removes most of the technical build time, generating a full landing page live in the video, but argues the real value was never the code, it's understanding who the customer is, what the offer is, and what's stopping them from buying, which is still work a person has to do. He suggests charging around £1,500 per page, plus ongoing support to keep it maintained.
best: Someone with a decent eye for what makes a page convert, a clear offer, a strong call to action, who's willing to do that judgment work on top of what the AI generates, rather than just shipping the AI's first draft.
truth: The £1,500 price point is the presenter's own suggestion rather than a documented sale. This is a similar underlying mechanic to other AI-website-building content in this space, with Framer as the specific tool of choice here, worth trying a couple of AI website builders yourself to see which workflow you prefer before committing to one.

name: Build a tiny niche AI tool as a subscription micro-SaaS
what: Instead of trying to build the next big app, use AI coding tools to build one very small tool that solves one specific, annoying problem for one type of professional, Hawksworth's examples include recruiters reformatting CVs or accountants answering the same client questions every week, then charge a small monthly subscription for it.
pitch: Hawksworth argues AI has dropped the technical barrier to building software low enough that you don't need to know how to code to get a working prototype, since the AI can write the code and explain the bugs as you go. He frames the real skill as spotting a narrow, annoying problem worth paying $30 to $50 a month to make disappear, arguing that revenue stacks up in a real way once you have enough individual subscribers, even at a low price point.
best: Someone who's identified one specific, recurring annoyance for one type of professional through direct experience or conversation, rather than someone guessing at a broad market need.
truth: The presenter doesn't cite a specific verified case study of this exact model working at scale within the video, it's presented as a logical extension of what AI coding tools now make possible, not a documented success story. The subscription price points ($30-50/month) are suggested starting points, not demonstrated market-tested prices.

name: Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE): freelance AI implementation consulting
cost: Low startup cost (no major upfront cost, time investment to build the skill)
what: Work as an independent "forward deployed engineer" (FDE), going on-site or remote with a business to deeply understand their actual workflows, then design and build the specific AI agents and automations that fit their exact processes, rather than selling a generic off-the-shelf AI tool.
pitch: Voss frames the opportunity around a shift in where AI's value lives: since every company now has access to roughly the same underlying AI models, the real edge is in how well that intelligence gets applied to a specific business's actual workflows, not the intelligence itself. He lays out a concrete 30-day roadmap to build the skill (build a working agent, harden it with guardrails and error handling, make it measurable, then rehearse pitching it) and a business model built around auditing a client's workflows first, sometimes for free to build trust, then charging for implementation, either a one-time fee or an ongoing monthly rate.
best: Someone with real technical comfort who's also a strong communicator, since Voss frames the job as equal parts engineering and the consulting-style skill of extracting how a business actually works from the people doing it.
truth: Voss discloses he runs his own company (Verity Agents) doing this work for large enterprise clients, so the roadmap is shaped by what's worked at that scale, not necessarily a solo freelancer's exact experience. He's candid that this is genuinely technical, multi-week work, not a quick weekend project, and recommends doing the first few client audits for free specifically to de-risk trust before charging real money.

name: Low-ticket digital course as a near-passive income stream
what: Package your existing knowledge into a low-priced digital course ($27 to $197), sold through an automated sales page and email sequence rather than live sales calls, so that once it's built it keeps generating revenue with essentially no ongoing fulfillment work from you.
pitch: Romero compares seven income models she's personally used, one-to-one coaching, high-ticket done-for-you services, low- and mid-ticket courses, affiliate marketing, brand deals, and joint ventures, and argues the low-ticket course model is the only one that gave her real passive income: she made $30,000 to $40,000 a month during a 90-day maternity leave without touching the business. Her reasoning is structural: no sales calls, no fulfillment, and it scales without needing more of her time, unlike the high-ticket, done-for-you offers that required a large team and heavy sales-call involvement.
best: Someone with real expertise or a track record in something specific who's comfortable creating an automated sales funnel once, rather than someone who prefers ongoing client relationships or high-touch coaching.
truth: Romero is candid about the tradeoffs of every model she covers, including admitting she got tempted into building a high-ticket, done-for-you offer that grew her team but not her margins the way she expected, a genuinely balanced account rather than a highlight reel. She promotes her own paid course (the AI Product to Profit Builder) partway through, worth knowing given how much of the video builds toward that pitch.

name: GoHighLevel AI setup for real estate agents (Zillow client sourcing)
what: Use Zillow's own agent directory to find real estate agents who are actively selling (filterable by top agent, buyer/seller agent, and area), build each one a free AI-generated website with an embedded AI chatbot trained on their listings and reviews, then convert the free build into a paid $299 to $997 a month retainer for ongoing lead follow-up and social content.
pitch: Wardrop, who says he worked with over 15,000 real estate agent clients from 2015 to 2021, walks through the exact mechanics: search Zillow's agent directory for a specific city, filter to top-performing agents since part-time agents likely can't afford the service, then use a single AI prompt to auto-generate a professional website, complete with a chatbot trained specifically on that agent's listings and reviews. The pitch to the agent is built on reciprocity, showing up with a finished, free website rather than asking for anything upfront.
best: Someone comfortable with a give-first outreach approach and willing to package one repeatable offer (website plus chatbot plus lead follow-up) that can be resold to agent after agent with minimal customization.
truth: Wardrop discloses he earns an affiliate commission from the AI software he's demonstrating and is promoting his own free workshop and course throughout the video. name: Shopify store creation as a service using Claude, Build Your Store, and AutoDS

name: AI-generated marketing kits as a standalone or bundled service

The underlying prompt-based approach is straightforward enough to test yourself with a free-tier AI tool before committing to selling it as a paid service.

name: Pet waste (dog poop) removal service
cost: Very low startup cost (~$500 for basic equipment)
what: Offer a recurring weekly service that shows up at a customer's home, cleans up dog waste from the yard, sanitizes the turf, and leaves, using simple tools: a rake, scoop, waste bins, disinfectant, and gloves.
pitch: Zaback cites U.S. pet-ownership data (66% of households own a pet, 65 million own at least one dog producing over 20 billion pounds of waste a year) and a real example he watched personally: a scooper who built a 300-customer route, did about 30 jobs a day per employee, and grossed roughly $20,000 a month, over a quarter million a year, charging an average of $69 per customer per month.
best: Someone comfortable with genuinely unglamorous, hands-on outdoor work who's building toward a recurring-revenue route rather than one-off jobs.
truth: The $20,000/month example is a single real operator Zaback says he personally observed and spoke with, a specific and checkable-in-principle account rather than an anonymous claim, though it's still one data point rather than an industry average. The pet-waste-removal market size and growth figures cited ($537 million market by 2035) are framed as industry projections, not something Zaback personally verified.

name: Pressure washing business with a trash can cleaning upsell
what: Pressure wash residential driveways, patios, and building exteriors, then add a simple upsell while already on-site: offer to clean the customer's outdoor trash cans for an extra $20 to $30 per can, since the water, cleaning solution, and equipment are already there.
pitch: Zaback cites a personal acquaintance, a former financial advisor with no industry background, who started with a trailer, water tank, hose, and surface cleaner, and crossed $100,000 in his best single month four years in. He frames the U.S. pressure washing industry as a $1.2 billion market across 32,000-plus companies with consistent, non-seasonal demand, and notes average residential jobs run $400 to $1,000.
best: Someone willing to start with used or basic equipment and build a route, then compound revenue per stop by bundling in the trash-can upsell rather than driving to new jobs for incremental income.
truth: The $100,000-month example is a specific person Zaback knows personally, a real but individual result rather than a typical outcome, and it came after four years of operating, not immediately. The trash-can upsell math (an extra $40-60 per stop) is a straightforward, independently testable idea regardless of how the broader pressure-washing business performs.

name: Trash can rollout and curb service
cost: Very low startup cost (no truck or special equipment needed)

That company reportedly has over 4,000 active subscriptions across 18 states with 500-plus runners, charging $49.99 a month per property, roughly $200,000 a month in recurring revenue, with a churn rate Zaback says is under 1%.
best: Someone looking for the lowest possible equipment barrier to entry, since the entire service requires no truck, tools, or inventory, just a route, a schedule, and consistency, well suited to elderly residents, second-home owners, and short-term rental turnovers as target customers.
truth: The company-level figures (4,000 subscriptions, sub-1% churn, $200K/month) are Zaback's account of a conversation with the founder during a business tour, a specific and named source rather than an anonymous claim, though not independently audited by Zaback himself. The core insight, that people will pay recurring fees for genuinely unglamorous, avoidable chores, is the same pattern that shows up across several ideas in this video.

name: Junk removal service
cost: Low startup cost (lower if you already own a truck)
what: Show up to a customer's home or property, quote the job on the spot based on volume, load unwanted furniture, appliances, or debris into a truck or trailer, and haul it away, getting paid in cash or card immediately rather than waiting on invoicing.

He emphasizes that the real growth lever is relationships, real estate agents, property managers, and estate sale companies, since apartment turnover alone runs 40-50% annually and creates a steady pipeline of clearance jobs.
best: Someone who already owns or can access a truck or trailer and is comfortable building referral relationships with property managers, agents, and contractors rather than relying purely on one-off individual customers.
truth: The per-day and per-job revenue figures are Zaback's own stated ranges rather than a single verified case study, though they're specific and consistent with the kind of pricing publicly discussed across the junk-removal industry. The relationship-based growth strategy (property managers, agents, estate companies) is a concrete, actionable, and independently testable approach regardless of the exact revenue figures.

name: Solar panel cleaning service
cost: Very low startup cost ($500-$800 for equipment, no license required in most states)
what: Clean the dirt, dust, pollen, and bird droppings that build up on residential and commercial solar panels, restoring lost power output, using a soft-wash or low-pressure hose system, a squeegee, and a water-fed pole, typically sold as a one-to-two-times-a-year recurring package.
pitch: Zaback frames the sales pitch around reframing the service: it's not just panel cleaning, it's recovering lost energy output on an investment that may have cost the homeowner $20,000-$30,000, since regular cleaning can boost power production by 10-20% in dirty conditions. He cites the solar panel cleaning industry being valued at $1.22 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $2.57 billion by 2035, with especially strong opportunity in high-solar-adoption states like Arizona, Texas, California, and Florida.
best: Someone in a solar-dense region looking for one of the lowest equipment costs and least regulatory friction on this whole list, ideal for someone wanting a simple, low-overhead recurring-revenue service.
truth: The industry valuation and growth figures are cited as third-party market research rather than Zaback's own data, and no specific individual operator's income is given for this particular idea, unlike several others in the video, so there's no personal case study to weigh here. The core value proposition (dirty panels underperform, cleaning restores output) is a straightforward, physically verifiable claim independent of any specific revenue projection.

name: Window cleaning service for homes and businesses
cost: Very low startup cost (~$500 for basic equipment)
what: Clean windows for homes, storefronts, and office buildings, starting with a basic kit (squeegee, mop, bucket, ladder, cleaning solution) and quoting jobs by square footage and number of stories, with the option to sell recurring quarterly packages to homeowners and monthly contracts to commercial clients.
pitch: Zaback cites an average residential job of around $550, meaning six jobs in a day already crosses $3,000 in gross revenue, and profiles an Arizona operator who did $392,000 in a year with a small subcontractor team, starting with just $500 in equipment. He specifically highlights commercial accounts (restaurants, retail, offices) as more valuable than residential ones because they prioritize reliability over price shopping and will commit to standing monthly contracts.
best: Someone comfortable quoting jobs quickly over the phone once they know their pricing formula, and willing to pursue commercial accounts specifically for the more stable, less price-sensitive recurring revenue they offer over one-off residential jobs.
truth: The $392,000/year figure is a specific, named example (an Arizona operator using a subcontractor team) rather than an anonymous claim, though it represents one successful operator, not a typical or guaranteed outcome. The distinction Zaback draws between residential (price-sensitive, one-time) and commercial (reliability-focused, recurring) customers is a genuinely useful and independently testable segmentation for anyone starting this business.

name: Pool cleaning and maintenance service
cost: Very low startup cost (a few hundred dollars for equipment)
what: Provide weekly pool maintenance, skimming the surface, brushing walls, occasionally vacuuming the floor, and adding chemicals as needed, for residential customers who don't want to maintain their own pool or risk it turning green and unusable.
pitch: Zaback cites the U.S. pool cleaning and maintenance market at $26.77 billion in 2025, projected to reach nearly $40 billion by 2030, and notes that most residential customers pay $100 to $150 a month for weekly service, a naturally recurring relationship since a neglected pool creates an urgent, visible problem the homeowner wants solved.
best: Someone in a warm-climate state (Florida, Texas, California, Arizona, and similar) willing to build a weekly route, since retention in this business is described as strong once a homeowner trusts a reliable cleaner.
truth: No specific individual case study or income example is given for this particular idea in the video, unlike several of the others, so the pricing and market-size figures are the only data points to evaluate rather than a personal account. The core mechanic (weekly visits, chemical costs scale with actual accounts rather than being paid upfront) is specific enough to verify independently before committing capital.

name: Lawn care and mowing route
cost: Low startup cost (one mower to start)
what: Build a residential lawn mowing and basic yard maintenance route, starting with one mower and expanding customer by customer within a tight geographic area to keep drive time low and route density high.

He notes the average U.S. household spends about $600 a year on lawn care, and that doing eight to ten lawns a day can generate $400 to $750 in daily revenue solo.
best: Someone willing to start small (one mower, one tight route) and treat this as a long, proven, unglamorous path rather than a fast or novel one, since Zaback frames it as one of the least flashy but most consistently reliable ideas on the list.
truth: The revenue figures are Zaback's general framework based on typical job counts and pricing rather than one specific named case study, unlike some of the other ideas in this video. The market fragmentation statistic (no company over 5% share) is a real, checkable structural fact about the industry that supports the claim of low competitive barriers, regardless of any individual operator's specific results.

name: Mobile car detailing service

best: Someone targeting busy professionals, luxury car owners, or multi-vehicle families who will pay a premium specifically to avoid driving somewhere and waiting, rather than competing purely on price with fixed-location car washes.
truth: The margin and pricing figures are presented as general industry figures rather than tied to one specific named operator's verified results, unlike some of the other ideas in this video. The core value proposition, that convenience commands a premium price people pay without much resistance, is a straightforward and testable claim independent of the specific dollar figures cited.

name: Claude Project skill system for end-to-end dropshipping store building

best: Someone who wants a fully guided, question-and-answer approach to starting a dropshipping store rather than researching each step (niche, product, store build, marketing) separately themselves.

The skill set and product database are distributed via a free cheat sheet that funnels into the presenter's broader AutoDS platform and paid product-sourcing tools, worth knowing since the workflow is built around that ecosystem.

name: AI-built dropshipping store with auto-loaded products and AI video ads

The AI video step specifically removes the traditional friction of dropshipping marketing, no need to own the product, film it, or hire an editor, since a single screenshot and prompt produces a finished vertical video.
best: A true beginner who wants the fastest possible path to a live, functioning store and is comfortable letting an automated supplier and AI tools handle product selection and content creation rather than doing deep niche research themselves.

name: Etsy print-on-demand business using AI-generated designs
cost: Very low startup cost (no inventory, pay only after a sale)
what: Sell print-on-demand products (t-shirts, mugs, posters) on Etsy by picking an evergreen, versatile product category, researching underserved niches and keywords using a tool like Alura to check search volume against competitor count, generating designs with an AI image tool like Midjourney, mocking them up in Canva, and connecting a print-on-demand supplier (the presenter uses Inkjoy) that only prints and ships once a customer actually buys.
pitch: The presenter, who's run print-on-demand since 2022, distills product selection into three criteria: evergreen (proven sellers like t-shirts and mugs that won't die out with a trend), profitable enough to be worth it ($8-10 per sale at a 20-30% margin is the target he uses), and versatile enough to carry designs across many different niches. He walks through a real example using Alura to check a competitor's fishing-t-shirt niche, finding it doing $3,000-4,000 in sales after 6-8 months with a manageable few thousand competing listings, and treats a competitor count under roughly 10,000 as a good opportunity signal.
best: Someone willing to do real upfront research (checking search volume and competition before committing to a niche) rather than guessing at designs, and comfortable using AI tools for the actual artwork even without traditional design skills.
truth: The presenter doesn't reveal his own specific niche, keywords, or exact numbers, citing competitive reasons, so the profitability framework and the fishing-niche example are demonstrations of the research method rather than his own personal, verified results. The specific tools recommended (Alura, Midjourney, Inkjoy) each cost money, roughly $10/month for the AI image generator plus Alura's own subscription, worth factoring into the very-low-cost framing.

name: Amazon Merch on Demand (passive t-shirt design uploads)
what: Create t-shirt designs and upload them to Amazon's own built-in Merch on Demand program, which creates the product listing, handles printing, shipping, and customer service entirely on Amazon's side, so the seller's only ongoing task is producing and uploading new designs.
pitch: Gottfried, who's run this program for nearly 10 years, explains the real leverage isn't in the small per-sale profit (about $3.18 on a $21.99 shirt) but in Amazon's existing shopper traffic doing the selling, since he's seen individual designs sell 400-700-plus times a month without any of the seller's own marketing. His top tip is checking that a design's exact phrase isn't trademark-protected before uploading, using a free trademark search, since a protected phrase can get a seller in trouble.
best: Someone comfortable treating this as a volume game, producing many designs rather than perfecting a few, and who's fine with the program's real barrier: an application to join, which isn't automatic.
truth: Gottfried discloses he sells zero physical products himself after 10 years of Amazon experience, everything he recommends is passive-income focused, which shapes which of Amazon's many programs he features. The per-shirt profit margin and per-design sales volume are specific, real figures from his own account, and the requirements (free to join, 18+, must live in an English-speaking country, no need to reside in the U.S.) are concrete and independently verifiable on Amazon's own signup page.

name: Amazon KDP low and medium-content books (word searches, log books, planners)
cost: Free to join, no ongoing fees
what: Publish functional, non-text-heavy books through Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing, word search books, log books, maintenance trackers, and similar niche-specific planners, using template-based design tools rather than writing full-length content, with Amazon handling printing, shipping, and customer service the same way it does for Merch on Demand.
pitch: Gottfried is candid that he tried full-length, text-based books and had little success with them, they took too long to create and weren't worth it for him, whereas low and medium-content books let him produce 5 to 10 finished books in a single day using template tools built for word searches, crosswords, and similar formats. Pricing works the same way as Merch on Demand: set a sale price, earn a few dollars in royalties per sale, and rely on Amazon's own traffic and volume rather than personal marketing.
best: Someone with no graphic design or writing background who wants a genuinely fast production process, since Gottfried emphasizes you can go from never having made a book to having one finished within a single tutorial session.
truth: Gottfried frames this specifically as "an even easier way" than typical KDP advice, which usually focuses on longer books, based on his own personal experience of what worked and didn't for him over years of trying different formats. Signup requirements are concrete and checkable (free, 18+, English-speaking country, no application required, unlike Merch on Demand), and no specific revenue figures are given for this particular business model in the video.

name: Amazon Associates affiliate income via YouTube review videos
cost: Free to join, no ongoing fees
what: Join the Amazon Associates program to get a unique tracked link for any Amazon product, then create YouTube videos (talking about or demonstrating products, without necessarily appearing on camera) with those affiliate links in the description, earning a commission on anything a viewer buys on Amazon within 24 hours of clicking through, not just the specific product featured.
pitch: Gottfried's single best piece of advice is to make videos about topics people are actively Googling or searching for on YouTube, since that content earns organic views without needing an existing subscriber base or following, and he notes that a large share of commissions actually come from "secondary sales," other items a visitor adds to their cart beyond the one they originally clicked through for.
best: Someone comfortable creating video content (camera-on or camera-off, talking about products they already know or own) but who doesn't want to build a large following first, since Gottfried's approach relies on search-driven discovery rather than an audience.
truth: Gottfried discloses that videos have worked "head and shoulders above everything else" for him personally compared to photos or social posts, a stated preference based on his own experience rather than a universal claim. The 24-hour attribution window and secondary-sales mechanic are concrete, verifiable facts about how the Amazon Associates program actually works, not marketing claims specific to his own results.

name: Amazon Influencer Program: short product review videos on Amazon listings
cost: Free to join (requires an active social media account to apply)
what: Record short review or demo videos for products you've already purchased from Amazon, upload them to your Amazon Influencer account, and earn a commission whenever a shopper watches your video directly on that product's Amazon listing page and then buys, without ever needing to post the videos to your own social media.
pitch: Gottfried, three months into this specific program at the time of filming, made about $70 in profit his first month simply reviewing products he already owned, then jumped to roughly $1,400 in his second month after switching strategy: using a data tool to check how many other influencer videos already exist for a given product (since Amazon only displays about five per listing) and prioritizing products with little existing video competition over ones already saturated with 100-plus competing videos.
best: Someone who already owns a range of Amazon-purchased products and is comfortable recording brief, simple review or demo videos, understanding that visibility (getting into the limited top-five video slots) matters more than production quality.
truth: Gottfried is specific that his own $70-to-$1,400 jump came from a single tactical shift (competition-checking before choosing which products to review), a concrete and replicable insight rather than a vague growth claim. The application does require proving an existing active social media account, even though the ongoing work happens entirely on Amazon's platform, a real and sometimes confusing requirement worth knowing upfront.

name: Building a high-ticket group coaching program from an existing YouTube channel
cost: Varies (mostly time; low direct cost to start)
what: A roadmap for creators who already have a YouTube channel and audience in a health, wealth, relationship, or serious-hobbyist niche (music, photography, and similar) to build and launch a group coaching program: survey and interview your existing viewers to find their top three problems and the false beliefs stopping them from buying, then build an offer, pricing, and sales page copy directly around what that research reveals rather than guessing.
pitch: Lawrence, who says he's generated eight figures from high-ticket programs and helped hundreds of creators with a claimed 90% success rate, illustrates the method with a real pivot: a client's planned generic "productivity" program was reshaped, after viewer surveys and calls revealed the audience was mostly high-pressure tech workers, into a program specifically about managing career pressure, which then sold out at over $5,000 per seat. He gives a specific readiness checklist (niche, comment engagement ratio, email list size and open rate, existing sales, and returning-viewer rate) and a concrete pricing tactic: start at a discounted "founding member" rate below your long-term target price to make the first launch feel less intimidating.
best: An existing content creator with a genuine, engaged audience (even a small one, Lawrence stresses total view count matters less than returning-viewer loyalty) who's willing to do direct audience research before building anything, rather than assuming they already know what their viewers want.
truth: Lawrence's headline outcomes (a program hitting $60K in six weeks, another reaching $100K/month in 120 days) are specific client examples he cites but doesn't independently document within the video itself, and he runs a paid tool and coaching offer that this video partly promotes. The core research method, surveys and calls to uncover real audience problems and objections before building an offer, is a general, independently applicable principle that doesn't require his specific program or tools to execute.

name: Organic (no paid ads) dropshipping via short-form video
cost: Very low startup cost (product cost plus website only, no ad spend)
what: Find a single simple, visually demonstrable product using a "burner account" research method (a fresh Instagram account that only likes and engages with product/ad content until the algorithm feeds you winning products), build a basic Shopify store around it, and grow sales purely through organic short-form video (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) with no paid advertising at all.
pitch: The presenter documents the process transparently over roughly 18 days, working exactly one hour a day: product research and ordering, building the store (using Claude and Gemini for AI-generated product photos), setting up social accounts, then filming, editing, and posting daily. He gives a concrete account-priming framework: post 4-6 times on a new Instagram account and watch for at least one video to cross 1,000 views, or scrap the account and start fresh with new (not reposted) content; Facebook uses the same rule but over 8-10 posts.
best: Someone with genuinely limited daily time who's picked a simple, visually self-explanatory product (an impulse-buy gadget, not something requiring a complex sales pitch) that can be filmed and edited in minutes.

He promotes his own free course and a paid one-on-one program at the end, but the documented numbers themselves are modest and specific rather than inflated, a genuinely honest case study by the standards of this space.

name: AI vibe-coded digital products sold through your own branded online shop
cost: Very low startup cost (AI coding tool plus a domain)
what: Research proven-selling digital templates and tools (using public sales-data tools to see exactly how many times a competing product has sold and for how much), "vibe code" a functional version using an AI coding platform like Hostinger Horizons, then sell it through your own branded .shop domain online store rather than a crowded third-party marketplace like Etsy.
pitch: The presenter shows real, specific examples to justify the approach: a finance-niche budget tracker template that's sold over 20,000 times for more than $400,000, and a life planner niched down specifically for neurodivergent people with ADHD that's sold over 22,000 times for more than $350,000, arguing that competitive niches (finance, health, productivity) are actually good signals of real demand as long as you niche the specific problem down far enough. She argues against selling on marketplaces like Etsy specifically because of listing and transaction fees, competition burying your listing, and the risk of account suspension, versus owning your own store with a .shop domain and full customer data control.
best: Someone comfortable using an AI coding tool with detailed, specific prompts (rather than vague requests) to build an actual functional product, not just a static file, and willing to set up their own branded storefront rather than relying on marketplace traffic.
truth: The specific $400K and $350K product examples are shown as public sales data from other sellers, not the presenter's own results, and she doesn't demonstrate her own product's sales figures within the video. She recommends Horizons specifically because it integrates with her own store-building workflow and is, by her account, one of the least expensive AI coding platforms, worth noting as a product preference rather than a neutral recommendation.

name: Interactive AI-native digital products built with vibe coding
cost: Low startup cost (requires a CRM/vibe-coding platform subscription)
what: Move beyond static digital products (PDFs, Canva templates) to interactive, AI-native tools built through vibe coding inside a platform like GoHighLevel's AI Studio: interactive workbooks that let a buyer voice-dictate answers and get auto-generated results, calculators (revenue, pricing, savings), client-tracking dashboards, bundles of custom marketing assets for a specific niche, and custom GPTs trained on your own expertise that a buyer can consult directly.
